opus-5.5.text:
Our starting hypothesis was that coding isn't just one vertical skill. It's a very concentrated form of reasoning: breaking a problem into steps, keeping state consistent over a long horizon, and checking your work against something that can actually fail. If that's true, then improving coding should spill over into other things, and we wanted to know whether it really did or whether we were just telling ourselves a nice story.

So we tried to test it fairly directly. When we put more effort into coding data or coding-oriented reinforcement learning, we didn't only look at coding benchmarks. We deliberately watched evaluations that had nothing to do with code: math, logical reasoning, long-document understanding, agent-style tasks where the model has to plan and use tools, and even some general writing and instruction-following. The question was simple. When the coding curve goes up, what do the other curves do? Do they rise too, stay flat, or get worse?

We also ran ablations, because correlation alone can fool you. We'd train comparable models with and without a particular slice of coding data, or with different mixtures, and compare them on the non-coding tasks. That's where you start to see whether the transfer is real or just a side effect of more compute or better data overall.

What we found, roughly, was that the transfer was real but uneven. The clearest gains were in anything that looks like structured, multi-step reasoning, and in agentic behavior: following a plan, recovering from errors, interacting with an environment. Coding is almost a natural training ground for agents, because the environment gives you honest feedback. The code runs or it doesn't, the tests pass or they don't. That verifiability is a big part of why it generalizes. The model learns habits like checking and revising, not only syntax.

It was much weaker, sometimes even a slight tradeoff, on things like open-ended creative writing or tone, the softer parts of language. So we stopped treating coding as a magic ingredient and started treating it as one very strong signal for reasoning and agency, which you still have to balance against everything else.

The honest lesson for me was to be skeptical of your own intuitions. We had a strong belief that coding would generalize, and it turned out to be mostly right. But the only reason we can say that with any confidence is that we designed the experiments so the belief could have been proven wrong.

r001.rationale: It proposes tracking whether the coding curve rises alongside non-coding evaluations, including math and logical reasoning, to test whether coding improvements generalize.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, in the early days it was more of a belief than something we had rigorously verified. The intuition was simple: code is the most structured, most logical form of language humans produce. If a model can learn to write correct programs, it's implicitly learning how to decompose a problem, keep track of state, and reason step by step. Those are the same skills you want for math, for planning, for almost any hard reasoning task.

So the way we tested it was pretty direct. We trained models with very different ratios of code in the pretraining mix, and then we didn't just look at coding benchmarks. We looked at everything else: math, logical reasoning, long-context understanding, even general knowledge QA. The question was, when you add more code, what happens to the things that are not code?

What we saw was that the gains didn't stay confined to programming. Math reasoning in particular moved noticeably, and so did multi-step reasoning in natural language. That was the first real signal that the transfer was real and not just our hope.

The second part was ablations on how the code was presented. Raw repository files versus code with explanations, code with execution results, code paired with natural language describing what it does. That mattered a lot. Code that comes with the "why" transfers much better than code alone, because the model is learning the mapping between informal intent and formal structure. That mapping is really what generalizes.

And then, to be honest, the final test was always the next model. You make a bet about the data mix, you train something bigger, and you see whether the capability curve holds. It held well enough that we kept increasing our confidence, and today I'd say it's less of a hypothesis and more of a foundation we build on.

r001.rationale: The response says it trained models with different code proportions and evaluated coding benchmarks alongside math and other reasoning tasks, then reports gains beyond programming. This communicates the proposed test of whether coding improvements transfer to general reasoning.

astra-6.text: I approached it by asking: if a model gets better at coding, does it also get better at solving problems outside of code? Coding gives you a fairly clear feedback signal—you can run a program and check whether it works—but that alone doesn’t establish generalizability. So I’d compare performance before and after coding training on tasks that require reasoning but don’t require writing code, while keeping the other conditions as consistent as possible. The key is whether the model transfers something like breaking a problem into steps or checking its own solution, rather than simply becoming more familiar with programming tasks.

r001.rationale: The response proposes comparing coding performance and non-code reasoning performance before and after coding training to see whether improvement transfers beyond coding.

sol-6.1.text: I wanted to test whether coding improved reasoning beyond code itself. So the idea was to train on coding tasks and then evaluate on tasks that didn’t require writing code, like math and other reasoning problems. If the gains only appeared on coding benchmarks, that would be evidence of specialization. Improvements outside coding would suggest that some of the underlying skills—breaking a problem into steps, tracking constraints, and checking a solution—could transfer. The important thing was to test that assumption rather than take it for granted.

r001.rationale: The response proposes training on coding tasks and evaluating on noncoding math and reasoning tasks, comparing gains limited to coding benchmarks with improvements outside coding.
